# How Is the SHSAT Scored? 2026 Raw, Scaled & Composite Guide


## TL;DR


The SHSAT is scored in three steps: your raw score (number of correct answers) is converted to a scaled score for each section, and those two scaled scores are added together into a composite score that ranges roughly from 200 to 800. There is no penalty for wrong answers. Cutoff scores change every year because admissions are purely competitive, with no fixed passing mark.


---


Understanding how the SHSAT is scored matters more than most families realize. The scoring system isn’t a simple percentage. It uses a non-linear conversion that can produce surprising results, where two students with the same total number of correct answers end up with different composite scores depending on how those answers are distributed across sections. This article breaks down every step of the process so you can set realistic targets and make sense of practice test results.


If you’re preparing for the SHSAT or another standardized exam, a[diagnostic test](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/diagnostic-test) is a strong starting point for identifying where you stand.


## What Is the SHSAT?


The Specialized High Schools Admissions Test is administered to eighth and ninth-grade students in New York City. It determines admission to eight of the city’s nine Specialized High Schools, including Stuyvesant, Bronx Science, and Brooklyn Tech. The test is developed and scored by Pearson Assessments on behalf of the NYC Department of Education.


In 2024, approximately 25,678 students took the SHSAT, and only 4,072 (about 15.9%) received qualifying scores. The test is given each October and November, with results released the following March.


## Step 1: Raw Score


Your raw score is simply the number of questions you answer correctly in each section: ELA (English Language Arts) and Math.


Each section contains 57 questions, but here’s the part that confuses most families: only 47 of those 57 questions are actually scored. The remaining 10 per section are “field test” items that the DOE uses to calibrate future exams. That means only 94 of the 114 total questions on the test count toward your score.


The catch? You cannot tell which questions are field test items and which are scored. They look identical. So the only sensible approach is to treat every single question as if it counts.


**There is no penalty for wrong answers.** A blank answer and a wrong answer are worth the same: zero points. Always guess if you’re unsure.


## Step 2: Scaled Score


Each section’s raw score is converted into a scaled score that falls between 100 and 400. This conversion is where things get less intuitive.


### Why Doesn’t the DOE Just Use Raw Scores?


Different test forms across different years can vary slightly in difficulty. A student who happens to get a harder version of the test shouldn’t be punished for it. The scaling process (called “equating” in psychometric terms) adjusts for these difficulty differences so that a given scaled score represents the same level of ability regardless of which test form a student received.


This is standard practice for major standardized tests. The SAT, GRE, and ACT all use similar equating methods. For more on how the[SAT scoring process](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/how-is-the-digital-sat-scored) works, see our detailed breakdown.


### The Conversion Is Non-Linear


This is the single most important thing to understand about how the SHSAT is scored. The raw-to-scaled conversion is not a straight line. Each additional correct answer is not worth the same number of scaled points.


Here’s an approximate example to illustrate:


- A raw score of 30 maps to roughly a scaled score of 248
- A raw score of 40 maps to roughly a scaled score of 300


That’s a 52-point scaled increase for 10 additional correct answers, about 5.2 scaled points per raw point in that band. But at the top of the range, each additional correct answer is worth significantly more scaled points. The curve compresses in the middle and steepens at the extremes.


The exact conversion table is proprietary. The NYC DOE does not publish it, and it changes every year as the test is re-equated. Old conversion charts from previous years are approximations at best and should not be treated as precise.


## Step 3: Composite Score


The composite score is what actually matters for admissions. It’s calculated by adding your ELA scaled score and your Math scaled score together.


**Composite = ELA Scaled Score + Math Scaled Score**


The theoretical range is 200 to 800, though DOE reports indicate that the practical maximum in any given year tends to be around 700, not 800. The range shifts slightly from year to year because of the equating process.


This single composite number is used to rank all applicants. Schools fill their seats from the top down, based on each student’s ranked school preferences. There is no fixed passing score. The last student admitted to a school in a given year establishes that year’s cutoff.


## 2026 SHSAT Cutoff Scores by School


Cutoffs shift annually depending on the applicant pool, seat availability, and test difficulty. Here are the official cutoff scores for fall 2026 entry:


School 2026 Cutoff Score


Stuyvesant High School 561


HSMSE at CCNY 539


Queens High School for the Sciences 531


Bronx High School of Science 525


Staten Island Technical High School 517


High School of American Studies at Lehman 507


Brooklyn Technical High School 506


Brooklyn Latin School 495


Historical data shows cutoffs typically move 2 to 10 points per year. Stuyvesant has ranged from roughly 556 to 566 in recent cycles. Brooklyn Tech and Brooklyn Latin sit at the lower end, generally in the 490s to low 500s. ## Why Non-Linear Scoring Creates a Section Strength Strategy


Here’s an insight that most SHSAT scoring guides skip entirely, and it has real implications for how students should prepare.


Because the scaled score curve is steeper at the top, excelling in one section produces disproportionately more composite points than performing moderately well in both. A student who gets 70% correct in both ELA and Math will score lower than a student who aces one section and gets only 40% in the other, even if their total number of correct answers is the same.


This happens because the scaling curve rewards high-end performance more generously per question. The practical takeaway: if a student has a clear strength in math or ELA, leaning into that strength during prep can be more point-efficient than trying to bring a weaker section up to average.


That said, this is a nuance for students already performing well. For students still building fundamentals, broad improvement across both sections remains the priority. ## What Changed With the 2026 Computer-Adaptive SHSAT


Starting with the fall 2026 administration, the SHSAT became a computer-adaptive test (CAT). This is the biggest structural change to the exam in years, and it directly affects how scores are generated, even though the DOE says the fundamental scoring steps remain the same.


### How Adaptive Testing Works


In a computer-adaptive format, the difficulty of questions adjusts based on a student’s responses as they progress through the test. Answer correctly, and the next question is likely harder. Answer incorrectly, and the next one is likely easier. The test zeroes in on a student’s ability level more efficiently than a fixed-form test can.


The 2026 SHSAT has 50 ELA questions and 50 Math questions (down from 57 per section), still totaling 180 minutes. Each subject still includes 10 unscored field-test items. The content areas, grade-level standards, and question types remain the same.


### How Adaptive Scoring Differs


Under the adaptive format, each question carries an established difficulty parameter placed on a common measurement scale. A student’s performance score is calculated based on the pattern of correct and incorrect responses relative to the difficulty of the questions they received, not just from a simple count of right answers.


This is powered by Item Response Theory (IRT), the same psychometric framework behind the SAT, GRE, and other major adaptive tests. As the test progresses, the student’s estimated score updates after each response. At the end, the final performance score is computed and then transformed into the reported SHSAT scaled score.


The DOE has stated that the scoring process is unchanged: raw score to scaled score to composite score. But the “raw score” in an adaptive context is more nuanced because it accounts for question difficulty, not just correctness.


### Navigation Rules Changed Too


Students must answer each question before advancing. Math items and standalone ELA items cannot be revisited once submitted. Within an ELA passage set, students can change answers until they submit the entire set. This is a significant shift from the paper test where students could skip around freely.


### What This Means for Practice Test Interpretation


Old raw-to-scaled conversion charts built for the previous fixed-form test are no longer accurate for the adaptive version. Practitioners on Reddit’s r/SHSAT have noted that families relying on outdated conversion tables will get misleading score estimates. If you’re using practice tests, make sure the scoring methodology matches the current format.

## The Discovery Program: A Scoring-Adjacent Pathway


Students who score just below a school’s official cutoff aren’t necessarily out of the running. The Discovery Program offers a conditional admission pathway for students from economically disadvantaged backgrounds or underrepresented middle schools.


Twenty percent of seats at each of the eight testing Specialized High Schools are reserved for Discovery Program students. To confirm the offer, students must attend and complete a free summer enrichment program at the school before ninth grade begins.


This is worth knowing because it means the effective cutoff for eligible students is somewhat lower than the published numbers. The program doesn’t change how the SHSAT is scored, but it does expand who gets admitted.


## What Is a Good SHSAT Score?


“Good” depends entirely on which school you’re targeting. A composite of 495 would have qualified a student for Brooklyn Latin in 2026 but fallen short at every other school. A score above 561 was needed for Stuyvesant.


As a rough framework:


- **495 to 510** : Competitive for Brooklyn Latin, Brooklyn Tech, HSAS
- **510 to 540** : Opens most schools including Staten Island Tech, Bronx Science, Queens Science, HSMSE
- **540+** : Competitive across all schools
- **561+** : Required for Stuyvesant in 2026


Fewer than 16% of all test-takers receive any offer at all, so every point matters. For a complete breakdown, see[what is a good SHSAT score](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/what-is-a-good-shsat-score-cutoffs-targets) .


## Score Release Timeline


The SHSAT is administered in October and November each year. Results come out the following March, along with high school admissions offers. There is no early score release or score preview. Students receive their composite score, their individual ELA and Math scaled scores, and their admissions result all at once.


Students who take the test in eighth grade and don’t receive an offer (or decline one) can retake the SHSAT in ninth grade, though ninth-grade seats are limited and cutoffs for those spots can differ.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is there a penalty for wrong answers on the SHSAT?


No. Only correct answers count toward your raw score. Wrong answers and blank answers are treated the same, so you should always answer every question, even if you’re guessing.


### How many questions on the SHSAT actually count toward my score?


On the pre-2026 format, 94 of 114 total questions are scored (47 per section). On the 2026 adaptive format, 80 of 100 questions are scored (40 per section). The remaining questions are unscored field-test items, and you cannot identify which ones they are.


### What is the highest possible SHSAT score?


The theoretical maximum composite is 800 (400 per section). In practice, the highest scores reported in any given year tend to cap around 700. The DOE has noted that SHSAT scores do not have a truly fixed maximum because the equating process recalibrates the scale annually.


### When do SHSAT scores come out?


Results are released each March, roughly four to five months after the test is administered in October or November.


### Does the 2026 adaptive format change how the SHSAT is scored?


The DOE says the fundamental steps remain the same: raw score, scaled score, composite score. But the underlying mechanics differ. In the adaptive version, your score depends on the difficulty of the questions you received, not just how many you answered correctly. Old conversion charts from the paper test will not apply.


### Can I retake the SHSAT?


Yes. Students who take the SHSAT in eighth grade can retake it in ninth grade. However, ninth-grade admissions offer fewer seats, and those cutoff scores may differ from the eighth-grade cutoffs.


### How is the SHSAT scored differently from the SAT?


Both tests use non-linear scaling and equating. The key difference is that the SHSAT produces a single composite used for a binary admissions decision (offer or no offer), while the SAT score is one factor among many in college admissions. The 2026 SHSAT now also uses computer-adaptive testing, similar to the digital SAT.


### Does guessing hurt my SHSAT score?


No. There is no guessing penalty. Leaving a question blank guarantees zero points for that question. A random guess at least gives you a chance of getting it right.
